p: And I would just add there that we have several programs specific on sort of, you know, previously disenfranchised communities, such as we have a women.nyc program that really provides sort of a network and technical support. We have construct NYC, which I mentioned in my testimony, and Waterfront Pathways that provides M/WBE, again, access to EDC projects, but also ongoing technical support, and the Founder Fellowship, which really looks to diverse entrepreneurship for these innovation industries.

Thank you. What are some of the metrics or the indicators that EDC uses to internally measure

success or impact on the City's broader economy? And how do those indicators look different in periods of strong growth versus weak growth?

Again, we have a whole social impact and sort of metrics that we look at, but what we strive to do is create good, high-paying quality jobs to support small businesses, to grow like industrial sector, innovation sectors for all New Yorkers, and to create a more affordable city for both residents as well as promote businesses coming here so that we can increase sort of our tax dollars to provide these services. So, that's sort of the overall mission of the economic growth that we look to, but we also, as I mentioned, have this economic snapshot and look at very specific indicators of employment and unemployment and labor force participation disaggregated by gender, race, and ethnicity, and we track that very closely just to see what trends are and the reasoning behind that. We track sort of the health of commercial and residential sectors in the city, as well as how tourism is doing and how people are using transit, so just the ongoing sort of economic activity of New York City. And if we see something that is changing

in a direction that we like, we don't like, we really try to dig in to see what's going on there.
The City's job numbers from the federal government are from January. How is EDC managing having outdated data when you're trying to assess current economic conditions?

Yeah. So, as I mentioned, we put out this snapshot monthly, but we haven't put it out since January for that very reason. Our next anticipated snapshot is going to come in April, but we pay attention to news, we see the trends, and we are very invested in the programs that we have in terms of making sure like workforce development, job creation, good paying jobs, and economic mobility are all part of everything we do.
I want to ask one more question on attracting new companies to New York and what strategies or incentives EDC has in place to support existing businesses, but also growth in those sectors.

Yeah. So, we have a couple of things that we do. First and foremost, we have an entire business development group that works, this is a free service, so to speak, of we do

outreach to companies that are considering coming to New York City, both in other parts of the U.S. and also globally, and we provide them connections to New York City. We give them like a one-on-one on the incentives that they might be able to access. In addition, we give site visits, and we might connect them to commercial brokers. So, this is an ongoing program that we have, and they're very, very active, and they're well known. We also have IDA, which is a discretionary incentive program that we have that works to attract companies to stay here and grow, reinvest here, or bring new companies here, and we really focus on the providing these tax incentives so these tax incentives are used as for like as a but-for argument, like before these tax incentives, this company would not move here, reinvest here, or grow here. So that's first and foremost, and we look at the return to the city, the jobs created, and sort of other community benefits that this company will bring.

Thank you. I want to acknowledge that we have our Finance Chair, Council Member Lee, here. Thank you.

I'm going to ask two questions about the Mayor's Management Report, and then turn to Council Member Lee for any questions that she might have. So, the Preliminary Mayor Management Report outlined that the previously reported value of the M/WBE award rate miscounted prime contractors and inflated the award rates for minority groups. Has EDC verified the calculations from that report, or the award rates for prior years, that they're correct?

Yeah. So, this was not a miscalculation of this award rate for M/WBEs. The PMMR is a very specific report that truncates the year for four months, so it doesn't capture a full year. We will put out an MMR, and it'll come out in September, and so I encourage you to review that, because that will have the real data. But the PMMR showed four months, so what happens is the M/WBE award rate is the amount of M/WBE awards we give over the total awards we give. And because it's only four months, it didn't capture the full denominator, so it didn't really capture the full value. But we do have a 35 percent M/WBE award rate goal, and in 2025, we had 35 percent of our sort of construction award rates go to M/WBEs, which was a value about 240

million. We anticipate sort of the goal being met at the end of this Fiscal Year as well.
Got it. So, on track for that 35 percent.
Yes.

Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. And another question on that report, the reporting period for the businesses served by industry-focused programmatic initiatives and people receiving skills training slash work experience through NYCEDC, the indicators that used to measure those things were changed, and data was not included in the PMMR. A little concerning about the exclusion of those metrics, so are there any key insights that would be helpful in shaping investments as we work through the 2027 budget, and can you speak to the reasoning for excluding those indicators in the report?

Yeah. This is a similar reason as the M/WBE award rate. Because it's only four months, it doesn't really capture, so the businesses that we serve or the people that we serve, and so what we asked the Mayor's Office is if we can

just look at it a full year, because most of that work is done towards the end of the year, so just looking at four months really understated the value of what we do. So, we have like 28 programs for the businesses we serve, and we have about 20 or so programs for the people that we serve in terms of work skills.
Thank you. Council Member Lee.
Thank you. Hi. Good afternoon.
Hi.

Just a few questions. First one on the tax expenditure efficiency. So, the Committee's interested in exploring possible savings in the City's tax expenditures, and we spend over 3.3 billion annually in tax breaks to encourage economic development in the city. And while much of this definitely represents commitments made that are important, and several years ago, many of the same tax incentive programs remain on the books and are unchanged from when they were developed in some cases decades ago. So, do you believe that each and every single one of

the City's existing economic development tax incentives are working as efficiently as they could, and if not, which do you think need improvement, and you know, how you're basing that information?

Thank you for that question. I think you're referring to the 3.3 billion I think is related to the Department of Finance statistics. We at EDC run the IDA Tax Incentive Discretionary program. So, just to give some background on IDA, a lot of the tax incentives that the State and the City give out are as-of-right tax incentives. IDA is a discretionary tax incentive tool that we use to, like I said, to bring businesses to New York City, have them grow in New York City if they're already here, or reinvest into their businesses in New York City. And we look at every single transaction individually to ensure that we're getting the best value, both return to City and jobs, through that transaction, and we negotiate very directly deal by deal with that counterparty company, and so to ensure that we're getting the maximum benefit. So, I think it's only about 330 million of the tax benefit that we have of the 3.3 billion that you're quoting. But we do think it's an important

tool because it's a flexible tool, and it allows us to attract business into New York City and have them grow here.
Okay. And which ones in particular do you think, from your vantage point, are working really well, that are working efficiently, and which ones perhaps need to be revisited?

We're open to looking at, you know, all the various tax incentives. Again, we only have the IDA Tax Incentive Program for the discretionary tax for private businesses, and we can apply that very flexibly. That's the other thing about IDA. It doesn't have to be for a particular sector. We can address whatever is the ongoing issue or the priorities of the City to attract certain companies or invest in, for example, the green economy is what we've done recently because we understand that combating climate change is really important. So, we can use those to attract companies and build those industries appropriately through IDA, but we're open to looking at other possible incentive programs.

Perfect. And you have the ability to, and ultimate responsibility for, ensuring that the economic tax breaks are relevant and efficient, right? So, if there is a need, if it's the environment this time around, but there's a new need that comes up, you guys have the discretion to be able to switch that, right?
Correct. And we look at every single, even if it's the same sector, we look at every single transaction and company.

Okay. Perfect. And I know that the Chair touched upon this, but going back to the discount rate and present value for the discount rates for multiple year tax breaks. Since Fiscal 2006, EDC has used a discount rate of 6.25 percent despite fluctuations in inflation and the overall interest rate environment. So, just wanted to make sure prior to Fiscal 2006, EDC used a higher discount rate of 7.75 percent and what motivated the change in the discount rate back then?

Yeah. So, we want to be in line with what OMB uses. OMB uses 6.25 percent, and we adjusted to be in line with them

because having different discount rates is confusing and we need to be uniform about it. So, I think it was a reflection of rates coming down, but essentially the discount rate reflects the opportunity cost of sort of investing that revenue and so we are very aligned with OMB on this.
Okay. And then when was the last time you reviewed the discount rate? Is it always the case where if OMB moves, you guys move also?
Yes.
Okay. And just wanted to get your thoughts on would it make sense or more sense to regularly update the discount rate to better reflect economic conditions?

I think it's really relative. I mean, I think, you know, as long as we're all using the same discount rate, if someone's using a higher discount rate, it's going to reflect the different value of the project than another one, so you can't compare the value of two different projects if you're using two different discount rates. So, I think what the primary, the goal is to use the same discount rate in order for us

to do comparisons of sort of the value of projects, not necessarily like changing the discount rate if the markets move like, you know, it's too much.
Right. So, not that it would be different because I hear you and you're saying that you need it be same as OMB, but in terms of the frequency of how often you look at them.
Yeah. I think we look at the direction of OMB and we want to be in line with them.
Okay. So, would you be able to make recommendations if the, you know, if that needs to be looked at in terms of timeline, right? So, if it's every one year, is it every five years, three years?
I can get back to you on how OMB looks at it. We take their direction.

Okay. And then just lastly, if I could, about the Chief Savings Officers. So, wanted to know if you have appointed the Chief Saving Officers, and are you able to share any other proposals for savings within the expense funding that EDC receives through SBS? And I know that your agency

is slightly different, so just wanting to see if that is the same mandate that you all have.

Yes. We were asked by City Hall and OMB to, like every other agency, to appoint a Chief Saving Officer at EDC, which we have, and so we're working with OMB and that submission should be, I believe, due this Friday.
Okay. And is it the same where it's 1.5 percent for '26?
Yes.
Okay. Are you considering potential revenue loss resulting from the implementation of the savings plan affecting net positive revenue programs?
No.
Okay. And are you considering changing any tax expenditures as a way to find savings? I'm assuming if it's…

No. As you know, EDC is sort of self-sufficient financially. We collect revenue on behalf of the City on our assets, and so we operationally sort of self-fund as well as do impact programs for the City.
Okay. Perfect. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you very much, Chair Lee. I am going to jump into some of the specific expense items that were addressed in your opening statement, and then we'll ask Council Member Brewer to ask her questions. So, the first is on the modular bathrooms. EDC released an RFP for the development of modular public bathrooms, and the request seeks proposals for designs of these modular units to be installed at various sites across the city, and the Preliminary Plan has four million dollars in support of this. The RFP closed in February, on the 24th, I believe, and I'm wondering if you can share any information about the number of bathrooms or anything about that plan so far.

Yeah. We were happy on behalf of the Mayor to work on the procurement for modular bathrooms to bring more public bathrooms throughout the five boroughs, and so we did put out that RFP. We're currently in the selection process with DOT and Parks as the bathrooms

will be on their sites at DOT and Park sites, and so we'll be getting back to you very quickly with that selection and information.
Looking forward to that. Is EDC responsible for selecting the locations of where the bathrooms will be placed?
The plan is currently being developed with really being charged by DOT and Parks but EDC is in collaboration with them along with City Hall.
So, is DOT responsible or Parks responsible for the locations.
It's like an interagency. I think the RFP just was clear that we wanted it across the five boroughs.
Is there any outreach being done to communities to determine which neighborhoods or communities need the bathrooms the most?
We were initially just doing the RFP and the procurement first and then there's going to be a plan that will be developed, again interagency.

Sounds good. Bathrooms are long-term investments. Could you give more information on why the City chose to have these listed as an expense rather than capital funding when presumably an investment in bathroom development could be capital eligible?

Yeah. So, capital eligible requirements are very strict. Modular bathrooms actually are not capital eligible so they needed to use CTL. The 4 million was allocated in the preliminary budget. It's because these are movable so they're not considered long-term infrastructure so they're not capital eligible.
Thank you. And I did have some questions on the City-owned grocery stores but wanted to pass to Council Member Brewer to ask your questions.
Thank you very, very much. I think you're doing fine. I don't know that you need anybody new. You're doing great.
Thank you.

I also love the internship, Rich Robbins' internship program,

whatever you call it, something fellowship and Essex Market. Those are two great EDC projects. Okay. So, there's a lot of discussion around the State and City budgets about corporate taxes and so my question they say New Jersey, you know, we're going to be not able to compete and then Mayor Bloomberg always said taxes don't determine where companies locate. So, I have about 10 questions. That's number one. Quick questions. What is your opinion on if we tax more corporations in the City of New York, how does that impact New Jersey competition, number one. Number two, where is my Brooklyn Bridge Beach? If you don't know about it, somebody here does know about it. I want to know where it's at. Number three, the Bloomingdale Library/project. People aren't happy with it. We want 100 percent, I think you know that, affordable. We like the library, blah, blah, blah, but we think it should be turned over to HPD as much as we like EDC. So, that's very, very controversial. I want to know if you would do that.

Three, lettuce washing machines. So, we're trying to get more upstate farmers to sell to the City of New York, but California has to provide the lettuce because they wash it. So, we need EDC to build us a lettuce washing machine so that the farmers can go to GrowNYC's hub at Hunts Point, you know, get the lettuce washed and then it could come to the schools and other places in New York City. I need a lettuce washing machine. I also want to just say that the hole in the ground when you did the issue with, you know, the place that you're talking about that you traded with Hunter College, you left a hole in the ground at 74th Street, and you own it, and I want to know what you're going to do. It's right near MSK. I want to know what you're going to do with that. And then also restrooms, I think it's great, but we did a report in the City Council last year and 63 percent of public restrooms now in the City of New York do not work or have repairs. So, can we use any of that very small amount of money, 4 million, to repair the restrooms or how do you look at the restrooms?

Those are just some of my questions. Thank you.
Okay. I'm going to try to tackle them.
Oh, helicopters. We don't like your helicopters going out of downtown.

Okay. Well, that's Anton, so I'm going to turn that over to Anton in a minute, but let's start with the restrooms. You know, I think everyone feels that there needs to be more public restrooms, so these are all good solutions. So, repairing the existing restrooms, those will be City capital eligible so, we are doing that, Parks is doing that, but this is not like a one --
Parks isn't. That's the problem. Just so you know. They're not putting any money into them.
Well, yeah. Parks is looking to try to invest in improving their public bathrooms, but that's a capital eligible project.
Yes.
This module bathroom is sort of different.
I understand, but the public, they stand out there and ask me that question, the public, because they like what's wrong.
Understood. All of these are sort of, you know, solutions that we're looking to.
I understand.
And East 73rd is, yes, we're going to be acquiring East 73rd. We haven't acquired it quite yet and we are going to --
What about the hole in the ground, which when you say East -73rd, what do you mean? I call it the hole in the ground. Go ahead.
Yes. That's our property. We're going to redevelop it into sort of institutional life sciences, but we're still working on a program to redevelop that site.
Do you have some timing on that? Because it was supposed to be part of Hunter College. Will they get anything out of it?
Yeah. Maybe we'll go back to you on that.
Does Josh has more information? Hunter College wanted to have sciences there because they don't have a great science space.
It's part of the whole life science redevelopment.
I understand that, but I'm trying to think about
Yes. So, CUNY is going to get SPARC Kips Bay, that's part of the SPARC campus, so they have a whole new --
A little bit, a little bit.
-- school there.
All right. When you're talking about East 73rd, I want to make sure that you at least consider also putting
Understood.
-- projects there. Okay.
The lettuce washing, we'll have to get back to you on that one (INAUDIBLE) and same with the Brooklyn Beach. Remind me the other question.
Yeah. So, what about New Jersey competition?

Oh, yeah. So, you know, again, as I mentioned, we have an economic research and policy group that tracks these things very closely. We don't opine upon sort of like tax changes in terms of policy, but we do track the impact of it, so we can do ongoing analysis, and we month to month, we track what the implications are.
Helicopters.
Okay. I'll turn it over to Anton.
Everybody doesn't like those damn helicopters.

Thank you for the question, and appreciate the… We certainly recognize the concern around helicopter noise and emissions for many New Yorkers. So, EDC, we manage two, for those who aren't familiar, there's three heliports in Manhattan. EDC is the agreement administrator for two of those heliports, and aviation and airspace in particular operates within a complex regulatory environment, as you can appreciate. So, the airspace is all federal, so there

are very limited local powers on where these aircraft can or cannot go. However, where we do have the ability, we are taking a number of steps. So, thanks to your leadership, Council Member Brewer, there was the 50 percent cut of 2015 levels that remains in place. We also limit the operating hours, and we've negotiated with industry-designated overwater tour routes as well. So, the tour helicopters that leave the Downtown Skyport, as we're calling it now, they stay over water, which cannot be said for aircraft that originate from heliports outside of the five boroughs. Now, in addition to this, we're looking forward to new technology on the horizon, this electric aviation or electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft. A couple points on that. As part of a 2023 announcement for a procurement of an operator at what was then known as a Downtown Manhattan Heliport.
We were there.

Yeah. We appreciated your attendance there. We demonstrated a piloted electric eVTOL flights with a leading European and leading American company, and you could

hear, or rather not hear, the improvements that has over traditional helicopters. So, we're leaning into that industry heavily. So, we made electrification a requirement at Downtown Skyport, and so we were selected Downtown Skyport, the operator, Skyport Infrastructure and Group ADP to electrify the heliport. I know you are familiar with a lot of these.
Every last bit of it. Go ahead. I could give the speech.

In addition to that, we also required blue highways build out with the City at Downtown Skyport. So, this is tying into the blue highways work and moving our freight from our roadways to our waterways. And then at the East 34th Street heliport, there was a five-year extension in 2024 that we also included this requirement to electrify. So, that's what we're doing…
What's the timing on this electrify? It's quite far in the future, I believe.

Potentially closer than we think. So, just a week

ago, we announced a joint New York/New Jersey application was selected by the U.S. Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration as one of eight kind of launch regions as part of the eVTOL integration pilot program. So, we're actively working with the private parties that develop these aircraft as well as our partner kind of agencies to safely integrate this technology into our skies.
I'm sorry, the timing?
The timing could --
A year, two years, three years, because meanwhile… Go ahead.
In terms of the EIPP program, there are provisions in place that could see, by the end of this year, certain kind of demonstrations and pilots that will inform the certification.

Okay. I mean, just saying people are just not, you know, going to the island, which is what they do in the summer. It's noisy. They're still flying over. They're not all

going over the waterway. I don't need to talk about this forever, but the numbers of complaints on 3-1-1 is the highest in ever. So, I mean, I know it's New Jersey. I went in that plane. I took the wheel, you know, the door off. I flew it. I got it. But you still have to curtail it or do something because of the complaints, I would suggest.

Yeah. And the tours, as you know, and the kind of airport shuttles are great initial use cases for this electric aviation just because of the distance. Our hope is by accommodating and welcoming this new technology, you can start to out-compete the traditional ladder helicopters.
We have buses and subways that go to the airports, just in case you didn't know. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Council Member Brewer. I have some follow-up questions, particularly on the 34th Street heliport, and then we'll turn to Council Member Riley. In the Preliminary Capital Plan, we have an additional 41 million over a 10-year period to

support the rehabilitation of the heliport, bringing the total City capital commitment to 52 million. My question is first, who owns the 34th Street heliport and what's the mechanics of the with Atlantic Aviation? This is building off of Council Member Brewer's questions.

Yeah. So, the City of New York owns the heliport, and EDC, through the maritime contract, is the agreement administrator, and the private operator is Atlantic Aviation. Now, to your earlier point on the capital, that's substructure work that is keeping the island of Manhattan upright, and it's more than just a heliport. So, it's stretching a number of sites to the north and a number of sites to the south.
That's helpful. How much revenue does EDC take in from its lease agreement with Atlantic Aviation for operation of the heliport, and is any of that remitted to the City?

Yeah. Thank you for the question. So, the way the fee structure is done, it's the greater of a minimum annual guarantee payment, which escalates depending

on the year. This year is one and a half million dollars, or 38 percent of gross receipts of the revenues collected. So, one and a half is what we're currently making. The heliport is actually operating significantly below capacity today.

And can you explain the breakdown of who's rehabilitating the 34th Street heliport, and how the additional funds are going to be applied? And is Atlantic Aviation committing any private funding to the to the project?

So, all the investment at the heliport itself is the responsibility of Atlantic Aviation. So, the electrification work, we put that onus on the private sector. The work that you're referencing is the substructure work throughout this stretch of waterfront, and we can get back to you with specific details on the contractors behind that if helpful.
That's helpful to clarify. Thank you. Council Member Riley.

So, good afternoon, and thank you, Chair Maloney, for your leadership. And I just want to share the same sentiments as

Council Member Brewer, saying that you guys are doing a tremendous job this morning. Thank you. I just want to spend some time with the World Cup. We know that it's coming very, very soon. And recently, the Administration allocated funding for activations and fan events. What are the primary goals for the additional 15 million dollars allocated for the FIFA World Cup? And how does the investment align with the City's broader economic and tourism strategies?

Yeah. Thank you for that question. This is going to be a very exciting time for the city. You know, we're again, like we're like a diverse immigrant community city, and so this is like the world sports that coming so I think it's gonna be very exciting for the city where it's going to generate an incredible economic impact to the city. We're estimating over 3 billion dollars from the World Cup activity. So, the 15 million specifically that was in the preliminary budget, we are working with the World Cup czar now to seeing how that's going to be deployed. But the sort of the primary goals for the World Cup is to promote the World Cup. EDC's prime

sort of role in that is to promote the World Cup. So, to get the word out that the World Cup is coming, get people excited about it, you're going to see flags, you're going to see murals, you're going to see banners sort of all across our EDC assets to engage the community prior to the World Cup, but also during the World Cup, like fan events and community-based programming, etc., watch parties, and then business attraction. Again, we really believe this is an incredible opportunity to highlight that New York City is open for business. And that is through not only companies coming from other parts of the U.S., but global companies are going to have delegations here. And so, we're going to actively work to make sure that they understand everything we have to offer.

Thank you. I'm really interested to hear about the small business engagement that you guys are going to be doing, especially within the outer boroughs. Want to make sure that majority is not even though Council Member Brewer is looking at me, majority is not in Manhattan. We want to get some love in the Bronx to make sure that they're utilizing some of the small

businesses out there as well. So, if you could just speak a little bit more how you're trying to get outer boroughs more engaged during the World Cup.

Absolutely. So, small businesses are sort of the backbone of the economy for New York City, and it's, you know, a tremendous part of all of our New York City assets. We have over 100 small businesses and all of our assets. We also have the public markets. So, the public markets has also La Marqueta in East Harlem, Essex Street, and Moore Street in Brooklyn. They also have about 100 small business and vendors. And all of that together, we're going to look at all of our sites, Coney Island, East New York, Kingsbridge, etc., just all across the city, especially in the outer boroughs, and we're going to activate those sites for the World Cup. And we really think this is going to bring both people in the community to like spend money, the small businesses in the community, but also bring people into that community to support the small businesses as well.

Thank you, Madam President.

I wanted to take a step and move to the modular bathrooms. I see right here that the Administration said 4 million dollars in funding. Is this 4 million dollars supposed to be invested in all the bathrooms that are being installed?
So, this 4 million is for a one-year contract.
Okay.
And so it is to bring online modular bathrooms throughout the five boroughs. And again, we're in this selection process, and so you'll see more announcements about that.
So, you don't have an anticipation of how much each bathroom will cost?
It's 4 million for all of the bathrooms. That's…

The only reason I'm asking, because I just spent, I think, 5.3 million on a bathroom in my District, and it was a comfort station in a park. So, I was just interested in seeing 4 million dollars here and seeing if you guys were just going to install one public bathroom.

No, no. I think the reason why we're doing these modular bathrooms is

sort of like innovative technology, is that the 4 million is going to deploy many bathrooms.
Okay. That's good. If we could talk about Hunts Point real quick. The money, can you speak about the phases on, I believe it was 240 million you stated that was going to Hunts Point?
For the Hunts Point produce market?
Yes.
It's about 405 million.
405 million. Excuse me. Can you discuss the phases on how that money will be implemented in this construction process?

Yes. So, the Hunts Point produce market will be an all new electric new facility so there's not really phases. It's going to be built all at once because you're not going to be decanting and moving people out. The current Hunts Point produce market is going to stay as is. We're going to build an all electric new facility right next door. And so, once that is fully online, hopefully by the end of 2029, the Hunts Point produce

market will move in there. We're doing it under a design build contract. So, we're hoping that that's going to move it quicker because…
Can you discuss the difference between that contract and the normal contract?
Yeah. Josh Kraus, who runs our capital team can sort of…
Thank you.

Yeah. Happily. So, I think generally speaking, the way that the City approaches things is what we call design bid build. So first there is a design consultant that is procured. They complete a design, and then the City goes back out separately to procure a construction contractor. And sometimes there are disadvantages to this because the contractor who's doing the work wasn't a participant in the process to design the facility. So, there are some gaps that sometimes occur. Also, there is the gap in time between when the design is complete and when the procurement for the construction can begin.

Under design build, these things are brought together as one so that you have a faster implementation and you don't have the ability for there to be any gaps between the design phase and the construction phase. So, that's why we're approaching it in this way. We think it will really help us to deliver this project in the most efficient, both time-efficient and cost-efficient way.
